source_refs.note: Book p. 179-181: 10.1.2 deductions 1-10, results (i)-(x). Book error: deduction 7 prints 'Let a = 2pi and b = phi' (working uses theta). Teaching notes, Exam tip, Key points, Common mistakes are ours.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: From the single law of 10.1.1 the book now deduces ten results, labelled (i) to (x). Each one comes from a clever substitution in a formula we already have. Keep these values ready: \(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0\), \(\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\), \(\cos 2\pi = 1\), \(\sin 2\pi = 0\), and for negative angles \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\), \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\).
Deduction 1

We know that:
\[\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
Putting \(\alpha = \frac{\pi}{2}\) in it, we get
\[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \beta\right)\]
\[= \cos\frac{\pi}{2}\cos\beta + \sin\frac{\pi}{2}\sin\beta\]
\[\Rightarrow \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \beta\right) = 0 \cdot \cos\beta + 1 \cdot \sin\beta\]
\(\left(\because \cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0,\ \sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 1\right)\)
Therefore

blocks.text_alt: cos of (pi over 2 minus beta) equals sin beta, result (i)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: \(\frac{\pi}{2} - \beta\) and \(\beta\) are complementary angles (their sum is \(90^{\circ}\)). Result (i) says: the cosine of an angle is the sine of its complement, for example \(\cos 60^{\circ} = \sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}\).
Deduction 2

We know that:
\[\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
Putting \(\beta = -\frac{\pi}{2}\) in it, we get
\[\cos\left[\alpha - \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right]\]
\[= \cos\alpha\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) + \sin\alpha\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\]
\[\Rightarrow \cos\left(\alpha + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos\alpha \cdot 0 + \sin\alpha(-1)\]
\(\left[\because \sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\sin\frac{\pi}{2} = -1\right.\),
\(\left.\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cos\frac{\pi}{2} = 0\right]\)
Therefore

blocks.text_alt: cos of (pi over 2 plus alpha) equals minus sin alpha, result (ii)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why is \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\) and \(\sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\)? The angle \(-\theta\) is \(\theta\) measured clockwise, so its point on the unit circle is the mirror image of \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) in the \(x\)-axis, namely \((\cos\theta, -\sin\theta)\). The \(x\)-coordinate (cos) is unchanged and the \(y\)-coordinate (sin) changes sign.
Deduction 3

We know that:
\[\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \beta\right) = \sin\beta \quad \text{[(i) above]}\]
Putting \(\beta = \frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\) in it, we get
\[\cos\left[\frac{\pi}{2} - \left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right)\right] = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right)\]
\[\Rightarrow \cos(-\alpha) = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right)\]
\[\Rightarrow \cos\alpha = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right)\]
\([\because \cos(-\alpha) = \cos\alpha]\)

blocks.text_alt: sin of (pi over 2 plus alpha) equals cos alpha, result (iii)

blocks.text: Deduction 4

We know that:
\[\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
Replacing \(\beta\) by \(-\beta\), we get
\[\cos[\alpha - (-\beta)] = \cos\alpha\cos(-\beta) + \sin\alpha\sin(-\beta)\]
\([\because \cos(-\beta) = \cos\beta,\ \sin(-\beta) = -\sin\beta]\)

blocks.text_alt: cos of (alpha plus beta) equals cos alpha cos beta minus sin alpha sin beta, result (iv)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Compare (iv) with the law: changing the sign inside the bracket changes the sign in the middle. \(\cos(\alpha - \beta)\) has \(+\), \(\cos(\alpha + \beta)\) has \(-\).
Deduction 5

We know that:
\[\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
Replacing \(\alpha\) by \(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\), we get
\[\cos\left[\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right) + \beta\right]\]
\[= \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right)\cos\beta - \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right)\sin\beta\]
\[\Rightarrow \cos\left[\frac{\pi}{2} + (\alpha + \beta)\right] = -\sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta\]
\[\Rightarrow -\sin(\alpha + \beta) = -[\sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta]\]
\(\therefore\)

blocks.text_alt: sin of (alpha plus beta) equals sin alpha cos beta plus cos alpha sin beta, result (v)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: How did the third line come? On the right we used (ii) \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right) = -\sin\alpha\) and (iii) \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \alpha\right) = \cos\alpha\). On the left, result (ii) with \(\alpha + \beta\) in place of \(\alpha\) gives \(\cos\left[\frac{\pi}{2} + (\alpha + \beta)\right] = -\sin(\alpha + \beta)\). Cancelling the minus signs gives (v).
Deduction 6

We know that:
\[\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta \quad \text{[from (v) above]}\]
Replacing \(\beta\) by \(-\beta\), we get
\[\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos(-\beta) + \cos\alpha\sin(-\beta)\]
\(\left\{\because \sin(-\beta) = -\sin\beta,\ \cos(-\beta) = \cos\beta\right.\)
\(\therefore\)

blocks.text_alt: sin of (alpha minus beta) equals sin alpha cos beta minus cos alpha sin beta, result (vi)

blocks.text: Deduction 7

We know that:
\[\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\]
Let \(\alpha = 2\pi\) and \(\beta = \varphi\)
\[\therefore \cos(2\pi - \theta) = \cos 2\pi\cos\theta + \sin 2\pi\sin\theta\]
\[= 1 \cdot \cos\theta + 0 \cdot \sin\theta\]
\(\because \cos 2\pi = 1,\ \sin 2\pi = 0\)
\[= \cos\theta \quad \text{(vii)}\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(\beta = \varphi\), but the working that follows uses \(\theta\). It should read: let \(\alpha = 2\pi\) and \(\beta = \theta\).
Deduction 8

We know that:
\[\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta\]
\[\sin(2\pi - \theta) = \sin 2\pi\cos\theta - \cos 2\pi\sin\theta\]
\[= 0 \cdot \cos\theta - 1 \cdot \sin\theta\]
\(\because \sin 2\pi = 0,\ \cos 2\pi = 1\)
\[= -\sin\theta \quad \text{(viii)}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Here the book puts \(\alpha = 2\pi\) and \(\beta = \theta\) in (vi) without saying so. Results (vii) and (viii) also follow from the fact that \(2\pi\) is a full turn: \(2\pi - \theta\) ends on the same line as \(-\theta\), so \(\cos(2\pi - \theta) = \cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\) and \(\sin(2\pi - \theta) = \sin(-\theta) = -\sin\theta\).
Deduction 9

\[\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \frac{\sin(\alpha + \beta)}{\cos(\alpha + \beta)}\]
\[= \frac{\sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta}\]
\[= \dfrac{\dfrac{\sin\alpha\cos\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta} + \dfrac{\cos\alpha\sin\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}}{\dfrac{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta} - \dfrac{\sin\alpha\sin\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}}\]
[Dividing numerator and denominator by \(\cos\alpha\cos\beta\)]

blocks.text_alt: tan of (alpha plus beta) equals (tan alpha plus tan beta) over (1 minus tan alpha tan beta), result (ix)

Deduction 10

\[\tan(\alpha - \beta) = \frac{\sin(\alpha - \beta)}{\cos(\alpha - \beta)}\]
\[= \frac{\sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta}\]
\[= \dfrac{\dfrac{\sin\alpha\cos\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta} - \dfrac{\cos\alpha\sin\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}}{\dfrac{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta} + \dfrac{\sin\alpha\sin\beta}{\cos\alpha\cos\beta}}\]
[Dividing numerator and denominator by \(\cos\alpha\cos\beta\)]

blocks.text_alt: tan of (alpha minus beta) equals (tan alpha minus tan beta) over (1 plus tan alpha tan beta), result (x)

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Quick use of (ix): \(\tan 75^{\circ} = \tan(45^{\circ} + 30^{\circ}) = \frac{1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} = \frac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{\sqrt{3} - 1} = 2 + \sqrt{3}\). (Our example, not the book's.)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\) (the law)
2. \(\cos(\alpha + \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta\) (iv)
3. \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\) (v)
4. \(\sin(\alpha - \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta - \cos\alpha\sin\beta\) (vi)
5. \(\tan(\alpha \pm \beta) = \frac{\tan\alpha \pm \tan\beta}{1 \mp \tan\alpha\tan\beta}\) (ix), (x)
6. Results (i), (ii), (iii), (vii), (viii) are first examples of allied angles, studied in 10.2.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Mixing the signs: \(\cos(\alpha + \beta)\) has a minus in the middle, \(\cos(\alpha - \beta)\) a plus; for sine the sign follows the bracket.
2. Writing \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha + \sin\beta\) or \(\tan(\alpha + \beta) = \tan\alpha + \tan\beta\). Test with \(\alpha = \beta = 45^{\circ}\): \(\sin 90^{\circ} = 1\), but \(\sin 45^{\circ} + \sin 45^{\circ} = \sqrt{2}\).
3. In the tan formulas, the denominator sign is the opposite of the numerator sign: \(1 - \tan\alpha\tan\beta\) for the sum, \(1 + \tan\alpha\tan\beta\) for the difference.
